Growing hearts from spinach leaves

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
......scientists turn a spinach leaf into a mini working heart

Unique Selling Point:
An amazing medical breakthrough that could in future save millions of lives

Summary:
Using plant-derived scaffolding, scientists built a mini version of a working heart, which may one day aid in tissue regeneration.

Further information:
Scientists have found a way to use spinach to build working human heart muscle, potentially solving a long-standing problem in efforts to repair damaged organs.

Their study, published this month by the journal Biomaterials, offers a new way to grow a vascular system, which has been a roadblock for tissue engineering.

Scientists have already created large-scale human tissue in a lab using methods like 3D printing, but it’s been much harder to grow the small, delicate blood vessels that are vital to tissue health.

“The main limiting factor for tissue engineering … is the lack of a vascular network,” says study co-author Joshua Gershlak, a graduate student at Worcester Polytechnic Institute (WPI) in Massachusetts, in a video describing the study. “Without that vascular network, you get a lot of tissue death.”

One of the defining traits of a leaf is the branching network of thin veins that delivers water and nutrients to its cells. Now, scientists have used plant veins to replicate the way blood moves through human tissue. The work involves modifying a spinach leaf in the lab to remove its plant cells, which leaves behind a frame made of cellulose.

“Cellulose is biocompatible [and] has been used in a wide variety of regenerative medicine applications, such as cartilage tissue engineering, bone tissue engineering, and wound healing,” the authors write in their paper.

The eventual goal is to be able to replace damaged tissue in patients who have had heart attacks or who have suffered other cardiac issues that prevent their hearts from contracting. Like blood vessels, the veins in the modified leaves would deliver oxygen to the entire swath of replacement tissue, which is crucial in generating new heart matter.

The study team says the same methods could be used with different types of plants to repair a variety of tissues in the body. For instance, swapping out the cells in wood might one day help fix human bones.

“We have a lot more work to do, but so far this is very promising,” study co-author Glenn Gaudette, also of WPI, says in a press statement. “Adapting abundant plants that farmers have been cultivating for thousands of years for use in tissue engineering could solve a host of problems limiting the field.”

Press Release:


Spinach Leaf Hearts
Scientists in the US have found a remarkable way to use spinach leaves to build working human heart muscle, which could provide a solution to repair damaged organs. By
stripping the cells of the leafy greens, the clear cellulose structure which remains, has the potential to mimic human tissue - perfect for a new heart. Carte Blanche explores
this extraordinary research.

Script:


V/O:
This is a mini beating human heart that was grown on a spinach leaf. In an unprecedented step, scientists at the Wuster Polytechnic Institute in the United States have managed to combine plant and animal tissue to create part of a human organ.
LINK:
If ever there was out of the box thinking in science this is it. And it could save millions of lives in the very near future.
V/O:
Graduate student Josh Gershlak and his supervisor Prof. Glenn Gaudette are working in the fields of bio-engineering and regenerative medicine. They published a paper in March this year that created quite a stir worldwide.
LINK:
In this paper, they announced a revolutionary solution to a very serious medical problem that claims countless lives all around the world.
V/O:
This problem is heart failure.
Josh:
Heart failure and cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death at least in the United States and I think rhird most world wide. It is a massive problem.
V/O:
It is such a massive problem because of the nature of our heart muscle. When a person suffers a heart attack blood supply to a portion of the heart is cut off, and the sections of tissue without blood supply, die.
Josh:
Cells in the heart do not proliferate, they do not multiply so what is dead stays dead, unfortunately. So whne someone undergoes a heart attack there is this large functioning scar. So when the heart works as pump it does not do so effectively as it once did. And this issue can lead to heart failure and death.
V/O:
For people with severe heart failure the only viable option to replace the dead heart tissue is to have a heart transplant.
Glenn:
And unfortunately there is not enough transplants available to meet that demand. So that is really the reason for regenerative medicine to try and regenerate tissue to replace the diseased tissue.
LINK:
For some years now scientists have been very successful in creating all kinds of tissue in the lab. They can even print blocks of tissue with bio-medical 3D printers.
V/O:
But so far scientists growing tissue in the lab have experienced a major obstacle.
Glenn:
As the cells, the tissue gets thicker and thicker get those cells will die if they do not get oxygen flow and that in our bodies is supplied through our blood, through our arteries. So that is what of the big limitations in regenerative medicine and tissue engineering today
V/O:
And so far, no scientist has been able to create a functional vascular system that could be used to supply lab grown tissue with blood.
LINK
One day Glenn attended a conference with other universities where they discussed the possibility of looking at the plant kingdom to assist with problems in human bio-engineering.
Glenn:
We took a step back and said well how does mother nature do it. How does nature make it gets nutrients and flow to all the cells in plants, for example.
V/O:
This was out of the box thinking, and Glenn decided to pursue it.
Josh:
So, one day he came to us and started talking about this crazy idea and we all looked at him as if he had two heads. And there was this one day when we had lunch and there was a piece of spinach and there was that vascular pattern.
V/O:
The very fine and intricate vascular system intrigued them, and they decided to look into it. But a green leaf could not be used in combination with mammalian tissue. Luckily both Glenn and Josh had ample experience with something called decellularization. It is a process of washing out and removing all cells from a piece of tissue or organ.
Josh:
We have done it with hearts before and it has been done by other labs for liver, lung, kidney, any type of tissue or organ in the body. Once you remove the cells through this process all that is left behind is that extracellular components of the tissue, that scaffolding, that framework of the tissue.
V/O:
Unsure if this procedure would work with plants, Josh volunteered to give it a try.
Josh:
I had a few decellurization already set up to work with hearts and what I did is I just stuck the spinach leaf in there with the needle through the stem and put it onto that setup and flowed through the same detergents and kind of washed it a little bit and saw some colour change.
V/O:
The experiment was a huge success. They were able to wash out all the plant cells from the leaves.
LINK:
But the big question was: was the network of veins in this newly created extracellular matrix still intact?
V/O:
To see if it was, they injected some red dye into the stem of the leaf.
Josh:
And that dye was just to show whether or not that vascular pattern was still open and worked after we did this process, which it does. Which was awesome. And another thing we did with that vascularity was to measure the size of that vascular network. So, we flowed through different size micro-particles and found that the micro-particles that were smaller and and on the same scale size as red blood cells flowed through. So theoretically blood would flow through freely
LINK:
So, they had a functional extracellular matrix with an intricate system of veins. But could it be combined with human cells?
V/O:
It is possible to grow large numbers of heart cells in the lab, and they found these cells readily attach themselves to the decellularized spinach leaves.
Glenn:
If you put enough heart cells together and if you have enough of the right cells they will start to contract. Our hearts have what is known as pacemaker cells and those cells tell the rest of the heart when to contract. And so, when we grow our cells here in the lab some of those pacemaker cells are also in our cells. If we have enough of them and if we have the right type, they will actually start to contract. And when have show that of we put those cells on a spinach leaf with all the plant cells removed, those cells still contract.
V/O:
They were also able to line the veins with a one cell thick layer of endothelial cells. These cells enable the veins to carry the necessary oxygen and nutrients to the heart muscle cells. So, in effect, they created a functioning mini heart from a spinach leaf!
LINK:
For now, the idea is not to recreate hearts, but to grow strips of functional, living heart muscle that can be transplanted onto diseased hearts.
V/O:
Large numbers of a patient’s own heart cells will be grown in the lab and then allowed to encase a leaf . And because the extracellular matrix contains no cells or DNA the body will not reject it.
Josh:
And so what we potentially would be able to do is grow a piece of heart tissue on the leaves and then replace that scar tissue in the heart with this functioning tissue and have that co-inside and bring back full function to that patient.
V/O:
If this becomes a reality, it will save millions of lives, and fewer heart transplants would be needed.
LINK:
And both Josh and Glenn are convinced that other plants will offer similar possibilities in future. It is already happening.
Glenn:
We have looked at using different plants for different needs. So for example our colleagues at the University of Wisconsin are currently looking at bamboo and decellularized bamboo to replace bone. We have also looked at stems that are large hollow tubes to replace arteries.
V/O:
And so, an innovative idea and a salad lunch could spell the start of an exciting new field in medicine.
Josh:
One of the big goals of this study in general was to really to kind of promote this idea of looking between the two kingdoms. Harnessing what mother nature has done with the plant kingdom and utilizing that towards what we need in our animal kingdom, providing solutions to some problems that we just can’t engineer the problems…. the answers to.
